questions.q: Per this lesson, why is a single overall pass/fail verdict considered less useful than domain-structured feedback?
options: Because pass/fail verdicts are always inaccurate
Because a result broken down by the same domains the board used to evaluate tells you exactly where to focus next, which an undifferentiated score can't
Because domain-structured feedback takes less time to produce
Because boards are not allowed to give an overall verdict at all
questions.explain: Reporting against specific evaluation domains (system architecture, security, data, integration, communication, etc.) tells a candidate precisely where to focus next -- a single overall pass/fail throws away that most useful part of the result.

questions.q: Per sources on Salesforce's CTA program, what does this lesson say happens when a candidate fails only one evaluated domain?
options: The candidate must wait indefinitely with no path to retake anything
The candidate automatically passes regardless of the failed domain
The program reportedly allows retaking a smaller, more targeted scenario focused on that specific gap, rather than redoing the entire multi-hour board from scratch
Failing any single domain always fails the entire exam with no retake option
questions.explain: Training sources describe section-level retakes focused on the specific failed domain -- this lesson also hedges that exact current mechanics should be checked against Salesforce's own candidate guide, consistent with earlier lessons' sourcing caution.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a 'design gap' and a 'performance gap' in feedback, per this lesson?
options: There is no real difference -- both require exactly the same fix
A performance gap always means the entire project failed

A design gap means the solution itself needs to change (a missing control, an unconsidered failure mode); a performance gap means the solution may have been fine but how it was presented, defended, or paced fell short
A design gap only applies to security-related feedback
questions.explain: A design gap requires revisiting the actual architecture; a performance gap requires revisiting presentation, defense, or time-budget practices -- conflating the two risks rebuilding a sound design or continuing to present a flawed one more smoothly, neither of which fixes the real issue.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend identifying a single highest-leverage gap rather than listing every piece of feedback as equally urgent?
options: Because trying to fix everything at once before the next attempt usually means fixing nothing well, while one clearly identified priority addressed thoroughly is more effective
Because only one piece of feedback is ever valid at a time
Because boards only ever give a single piece of feedback total
Because prioritizing feedback is required by Salesforce's exam rules
questions.explain: The structured debrief method specifically calls for identifying the single highest-leverage gap, since attempting to fix every gap at once typically results in none of them being addressed thoroughly before the next attempt.

questions.q: How does this lesson explicitly connect back to Lesson 1?
options: It contradicts Lesson 1's description of what an ARB evaluates
It notes that every piece of feedback from a real board maps back to one of the original evaluation domains Lesson 1 established, closing the loop from definition through practice to iteration
It states that Lesson 1's material is no longer relevant by this point in the course
It introduces a completely new, unrelated set of evaluation domains
questions.explain: This lesson explicitly closes the loop: the evaluation domains defined in Lesson 1 are the same categories feedback is structured against here, turning the course's material into a cycle of practice and structured improvement rather than a one-time read.
